edges: Caesar’s fine is the first sign in the sources of the scale of Leptis’s oil, which Mattingly takes to be Lepcis Magna’s.
Mattingly links the surplus oil of the Tripolitanian estates to the stamped amphorae that reached Rome and Ostia.
Mattingly reads the oil donation and the oil procurator as consequences of the elite’s oil wealth and of Severus’s favour.
Monte Testaccio is where the emptied jars from Spain and Africa were dumped; Tripolitanian stamps appear there too.
Rodríguez Almeida’s figure for Rome’s imports and the per-head rule of thumb are two attempts to size the same oil economy.
The beam and screw presses of the sources are the machines that the Tripolitanian press sites housed, though Mattingly’s survey does not name their type.
Needham sets the Roman presses against China’s late adoption of pressing as the contrast the folio reads across.
Mattingly counts soaps, perfumes and medicaments among the uses that make oil’s importance underestimated.
Both are Roman-world remarks on northern butter use, Sidonius as insult and Galen as medicine.
Mueller’s northern animal-fat culture is the one Sidonius mocks, in Gaul, in the 470s.
Anthimus, at the Ostrogothic court, writes of butter and lard as the northerners use them.
The ghee and sesame oil of the Periplus are the fats that Caraka’s medicine prescribes by season.
Anthimus’s butter cure continues the medical use of butter that Galen records.
The Vinaya’s five medicines and the Caraka’s seasonal rule for ghee are two early Indian prescriptions of fats as medicine.
The Charaka and Arthaśāstra describe the same shift from ghee to oil as cooking medium in the early centuries AD.
Sesame’s arrival and the late-Han pressing of seeds fall in the same period, though Needham says sesame pressing is not mentioned before the Song.
Needham reads the Po wu chi’s oil stored by the ten thousand piculs as the next trace of oil as a commodity after the Han pressing.
The same sixth-century farm manual that records colza oil mills gives the recipe for churning su.
The warehouse of c.290 and the colza mills of 544 are successive stages of the Chinese oil trade in Needham’s account.
The Indian Ocean trade in ghee and sesame oil and the Pacific island coconut are the two tropical fat economies outside the Roman world.
Mago’s manual and the Lepcis oil fine both come from the Carthaginian lands that Rome took in 146 BC and 46 BC.
Delos’s oil prices and the Roman world’s per-head oil use are two ways of asking how a city fed itself with oil.
Hanukkah’s lamp oil and the Buddha’s five medicines are two religions making a fat a sacred ration.
The oils named in the Fayum papyri are the oils Ptolemy II’s tax in the same century singled out.
